steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on Pink, a multi-modal LLM whose fine-grained image perception we improve through referential comprehension tasks. It should explain why current MLLMs struggle with fine-grained understanding, then describe our dataset construction pipeline, how we tune the visual encoder, and our main results and contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- LLMs extended to MLLMs; still weak at fine-grained image understanding
- Existing RC datasets are not enough for instruction tuning
- Visual encoder is a bottleneck
- Our framework (Pink): RC task pipeline + self-consistent bootstrapping
- Tuning the visual encoder with Adapters / LoRA
- Experiments and results
- Summary of contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- LLMs and MLLMs
  - LLMs (cite): impressive on wide range of NL tasks
  - extended to MLLMs with other modalities: image, audio, point cloud
  - visual instruction tuning (cite): high-quality image-text instruction data, project visual features into LLM language space (cite)
  - basic image-level comprehension ok, fine-grained understanding still a problem (cite)
  - limits multi-modal performance and applications, see GPT-4V(ision) test report (cite)
- RC datasets
  - some methods (cite) add Referential Comprehension (RC) data: RefCOCO (cite), PointQA (cite)
  - not enough to cover abilities needed for fine-grained perception
  - few RC tasks -> hard to generalize across RC tasks
  - Fig. 4: Shikra (cite), Qwen-VL (cite) poor instruction following on RC tasks outside their tuning, irrelevant answers
- Visual encoder
  - usually trained with contrastive language-image pre-training as in CLIP (cite)
  - global alignment does not capture region-word relationships (cite)
  - encoder = bottleneck for fine-grained perception
- Pink
  - new framework, enhance fine-grained perception via RC tasks; model called Pink
  - fundamental abilities: instance identification, relative positions between instances
  - dataset construction pipeline: extend existing annotations to RC tasks
  - tasks e.g. visual relation reasoning, visual spatial reasoning, from Visual Genome (cite) annotations
  - self-consistent bootstrapping: dense object annotations -> referring-expression-bounding-box pairs
  - vs. expensive, uncontrollable GPT4 API data generation (cite); high-quality data, precise enhancement
  - Fig. 1: good performance with fewer training samples
- Visual encoder tuning
  - most MLLMs freeze encoder during instruction tuning (cite)
  - direct tuning -> semantic loss, small instruction dataset (cite)
  - add tunable components: Adapters (cite), LoRA (cite)
  - main parameters frozen -> no forgetting; components adapt the encoder
- Experiments
  - better on conventional vision-language tasks and RC tasks
  - 6.7M tunable params, up to 6.0% accuracy gain on OK-VQA (cite) vs Shikra (cite)
  - top rank on MMBench (cite) leaderboard
  - beats methods with more training data, e.g. Qwen-VL (cite)
- Contributions
  - two bottlenecks: limited instruction tuning tasks, weak visual encoder
  - any dataset with annotations -> instruction tuning data; bootstrapping adds more
  - lower cost, diverse tasks, no GPT4 API dependency
  - reproducible: public data, consumer GPUs with 24GB memory
  - release code and datasets

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive capabilities on lots of different natural language tasks. Because of these results, researchers have tried to extend LLMs into Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by adding other modalities like image, audio, or point cloud. Just doing global alignment does not work well for finding the fine-grained relationships between image regions and text words. So the visual encoder is a bottleneck for fine-grained image perception in MLLMs.

  - fundamental abilities: instance identification, relative positions between instances -> include in instruction tuning
  - dataset construction pipeline extends existing annotations to RC tasks, e.g. visual relation reasoning, visual spatial reasoning (Visual Genome annotations)
  - self-consistent bootstrapping: dense object annotations -> referring-expression-bounding-box pairs
  - vs. GPT4 API generation (expensive, uncontrollable); high-quality data; Fig. 1 fewer training samples
- Visual encoder tuning
  - most MLLMs freeze encoder; direct tuning -> semantic loss (small dataset)
  - Adapters, LoRA; main params frozen, no forgetting
- Experiments
  - better on conventional VL and RC tasks
  - 6.7M tunable params, up to 6.0% on OK-VQA vs Shikra; top of MMBench leaderboard; beats Qwen-VL with more data

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive capabilities on lots of different natural language tasks. Because of these results, researchers have tried to extend LLMs into Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by adding other modalities like image, audio, or point cloud. Visual instruction tuning uses high-quality image-text instruction tuning data, and it lets the LLM get visual comprehension ability by projecting the visual features into the natural language space of the LLM. With these methods, existing MLLMs can do basic image-level comprehension. But they still have problems with fine-grained image understanding. This limited fine-grained understanding hurts the performance of MLLMs on multi-modal tasks and also restricts their possible applications, as the GPT-4V(ision) test report also shows.

To deal with this, some methods add datasets about Referential Comprehension (RC), like RefCOCO and PointQA, to improve the fine-grained image perception of MLLMs. However these datasets are not enough to cover the wide range of abilities that MLLMs need for fine-grained image perception. Having only a few RC tasks also makes it hard for the model to generalize to different RC tasks through instruction tuning. For example, in Fig. 4, Shikra and Qwen-VL show limited instruction-following ability on RC tasks that were not in their instruction tuning, and they fail to give relevant answers to the questions.

Besides instruction tuning, the visual encoder is also important for the performance of MLLMs. MLLMs usually use a visual encoder trained with contrastive language-image pre-training, like the one in CLIP. Just doing global alignment does not work well for finding the fine-grained relationships between image regions and text words. So the visual encoder is a bottleneck for fine-grained image perception in MLLMs.

In this paper we propose a new framework that improves the fine-grained image perception ability of MLLMs using RC tasks, and we call the trained model Pink. Fine-grained image understanding is closely related to some fundamental abilities, like identifying instances and recognizing the relative positions between different instances. So it is important to put tasks that need these fundamental abilities into instruction tuning, in order to improve the fine-grained perception of the model. For this we propose a new dataset construction pipeline that extends the annotations of existing datasets into various RC tasks about these abilities. More specifically, we design several RC tasks, for example visual relation reasoning and visual spatial reasoning, using the annotations from Visual Genome. To get even more training data for these RC tasks, we also introduce a new self-consistent bootstrapping method that extends dense object annotations into referring-expression-bounding-box pairs. Generating data with the GPT4 API is expensive and uncontrollable, while our method uses the annotations that already exist in datasets. This gives high-quality data and precisely enhances the capabilities that the model needs. In Fig. 1, the high-quality instruction tuning data from our method lets the model get promising performance with fewer training samples.

Improving the fine-grained understanding ability of the visual encoder is not trivial. Most existing MLLMs freeze the visual encoder during instruction tuning. This is because tuning the visual encoder directly can lead to semantic loss, since the visual instruction dataset is limited in scale. To solve this we tune the visual encoder by adding some tunable components like Adapters and LoRA. The main parameters of the model are frozen, so the learned knowledge is not forgotten, and the added tunable components are trained to adapt the visual encoder.

We did extensive experiments to test the performance of the model. Thanks to the tasks we designed for instruction tuning, our framework improves the performance of MLLMs both on conventional vision-language tasks and on RC tasks. For example, with only 6.7M tunable parameters, we get up to a 6.0% accuracy improvement on OK-VQA compared to Shikra. We also get the top rank on the MMBench leaderboard. Our method also does better than methods that use more training data, e.g., Qwen-VL.

This work is an original effort to improve the fine-grained image perception of MLLMs, and it addresses two main bottlenecks: the limited instruction tuning tasks and the lack of ability of the visual encoder. Because we design tasks related to fundamental abilities, any dataset that has the corresponding annotations can be turned into an instruction tuning dataset. The self-consistent bootstrapping increases the amount of training data even more. This pipeline greatly reduces the cost of getting high-quality data with diverse tasks, and it removes the dependency on GPT4 APIs. The whole training pipeline can be reproduced in academia, because it only uses publicly available data and can be trained on consumer GPUs with 24GB memory. We will release the codes and datasets to help further research and evaluation.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) [1,2,3,4] show impressive capabilities across a wide range of natural language tasks. These results have motivated researchers to extend LLMs to Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by integrating additional modalities, e.g., image, audio, or point cloud. Visual instruction tuning [5,6,7], which uses high-quality image-text instruction tuning data, incorporates visual comprehension ability into LLMs by projecting visual features into the natural language space of the LLMs [8]. Powered by these methods, existing MLLMs are capable of basic image-level comprehension. However, they still struggle with fine-grained image understanding [9,10,11]. Limited fine-grained image understanding ability hinders the performance of MLLMs in multi-modal tasks and restricts their potential applications, as reported in the GPT-4V(ision) test report [12].

To address this issue, some methods [13,14] incorporate datasets related to Referential Comprehension (RC) such as RefCOCO [11] and PointQA [15] to enhance the fine-grained image perception ability of MLLMs. However, these datasets are insufficient to cover the wide range of abilities that MLLMs need for fine-grained image perception. Limited RC tasks also make it hard for the model to generalize across various RC tasks through instruction tuning. For instance, as shown in Fig. 4, Shikra [13] and Qwen-VL [16] show limited instruction-following ability on RC tasks beyond their instruction tuning, failing to provide relevant responses to questions.

Beyond instruction tuning, the capability of the visual encoder is also important to the performance of MLLMs. MLLMs typically employ a visual encoder trained through contrastive language-image pre-training like the one in CLIP [17]. Simply performing global alignment is ineffective at exploring fine-grained relationships between image regions and text words [18,19]. The visual encoder is thus a bottleneck for achieving fine-grained image perception in MLLMs.

This paper proposes a new framework to enhance the fine-grained image perception ability of MLLMs through RC tasks. We refer to the trained model as Pink. Fine-grained image understanding is closely tied to fundamental abilities such as instance identification and recognition of relative positions between different instances. Integrating tasks that demand these abilities during instruction tuning is therefore crucial for enhancing the model's fine-grained image perception. To this end, we propose a new dataset construction pipeline that extends the annotations of existing datasets to various RC tasks about these fundamental abilities. Specifically, we design several RC tasks, such as visual relation reasoning and visual spatial reasoning, based on the annotations from Visual Genome [20]. To incorporate more training data for these RC tasks, we further introduce a novel self-consistent bootstrapping method that extends dense object annotations to referring-expression-bounding-box pairs. Compared to the expensive and uncontrollable process of generating data with the GPT4 API [13,21], our method leverages existing dataset annotations. This results in high-quality data and a precise enhancement of the capabilities the model needs. As shown in Fig. 1, the high-quality instruction tuning data generated by our method allows the model to achieve promising performance with fewer training samples.

Improving the fine-grained image understanding ability of the visual encoder is not trivial. Most existing MLLMs [22,5,7,13,6] freeze the visual encoder during instruction tuning, because directly tuning it can cause semantic loss given the limited scale of the visual instruction dataset [23]. To address this issue, we tune the visual encoder by introducing several tunable components such as Adapters [24] and LoRA [25]. Freezing the main parameters of the model avoids forgetting learned knowledge, while the introduced components are trained to adapt the visual encoder.

We have conducted extensive experiments to test the performance of the model. Benefiting from the tasks designed for instruction tuning, our framework enhances MLLMs' performance in both conventional vision-language tasks and RC tasks. For instance, with only 6.7M tunable parameters, we achieve up to a 6.0% accuracy improvement on OK-VQA [26] compared to Shikra [13]. We also attain the top rank on the leaderboard of MMBench [27]. Notably, our method also surpasses methods that rely on more training data, e.g., Qwen-VL [16].

This work is an original effort to enhance MLLMs' fine-grained image perception ability by addressing two main bottlenecks: limited instruction tuning tasks and the limited ability of the visual encoder. By designing tasks related to fundamental abilities, any dataset with corresponding annotations can be converted into an instruction tuning dataset, and the self-consistent bootstrapping further increases the amount of training data. This pipeline significantly reduces the cost of obtaining high-quality data with diversified tasks and eliminates the dependency on GPT4 APIs. The whole training pipeline is reproducible in academia, as it relies only on publicly available data and can be trained on consumer GPUs with 24GB memory. We will release the codes and datasets to facilitate further research and evaluation.
